stimulus.text:
“To-day three-fourths of its people live in the tenements, and the nineteenth century drift of the population to the cities is sending ever-increasing multitudes to crowd them. The fifteen thousand tenant houses that were the despair of the sanitarian in the past generation have swelled into thirty-seven thousand, and more than twelve hundred thousand persons call them home.”

Jacob A. Riis, How the Other Half Lives (1890), Introduction.
stimulus.source_note: Jacob A. Riis, How the Other Half Lives (New York: Charles Scribner’s Sons, 1890), Introduction. Public domain; text checked against Project Gutenberg eBook 45502.

source: original; stimulus verified against its source (see source_note)

books.section: Topic 6.8 Immigration and Migration in the Gilded Age

primary_sources: Jacob A. Riis, How the Other Half Lives (1890)

stem: Riis says the number of tenant houses grew from fifteen thousand to thirty-seven thousand. That growth best shows what?

options.text: That tenements were disappearing as the city grew
options.misconception: Reads a rise in tenement numbers as a fall.

options.text: That most New Yorkers had moved to the suburbs
options.misconception: Reverses the drift: people moved into the city, not out.

options.text: That tenement crowding grew worse as the city grew
That the city had solved its housing problem
options.misconception: Treats a growing housing problem as a solved one.

rationales.A: The number rose from fifteen thousand to thirty-seven thousand. Tenements were spreading, not disappearing.
rationales.B: Riis says the drift of population was into the cities, not out to the suburbs.
rationales.C: More tenant houses holding ever-increasing multitudes means the crowding grew worse, not better.
rationales.D: A rise to thirty-seven thousand tenant houses is a growing problem, not a solved one.
rationales.general:
Ask what a rising number means.
1. Tenant houses more than doubled, from fifteen thousand to thirty-seven thousand.
2. At the same time, ever-increasing multitudes crowded into them.
3. More houses plus more people means the crowding grew worse.
4. A problem that grows is not a problem that is solved.
Remember: a rising count plus rising crowding means a worsening problem.
